MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: Despite a wave of Iranian attacks since the beginning of October, total Middle Eastern crude oil flows (ex-Iran) remain resilient. Flows are becoming, however, lumpier (days of multiple tanker crossings followed by days of very few tankers). 

Overall, Middle East (ex-Iran) crude flows, including Strait of Hormuz plus all the bypass routes, are holding at ~75% of pre-war levels, down from a ~95% *peak* in the last days of September. Crucially, despite the drop in recent days, the Oct 1-Oct 10 period average remains above Sep full month average (and well above full month August). Kuwait is struggling the most right now. UAE, Iraq and KSA (the last one using both Persian Gulf and Red Sea) are doing relatively well.

All said, the risk is to the downside if the Iranian attacks continue (and if they become more successful). Iran has sunk at least one container ship in the SoH over the last 24 hours. The same goes for Red Sea flows under Houthi / Iraq militias potential attacks. For Iran itself, Hormuz remains closed.

One key indicator to follow: despite the Iranian attacks against SoH traffic, the physical premium for Middle Eastern crude has come down significantly in recent days, touching today a near 2½-month low.

Over the past decade, energy has been the sector where you throw your career away. For those of us who survived, the numerous battle scars can fill a bookshelf. I can’t count how many times I thought about quitting. You can read through the archive in the “memo” tab to get a glimpse of the pain we all had to go through.

But now that energy is front and center in the global investing landscape, most people are still choosing to ignore it because it’s transitory. IEA, the energy agency created to help the world avoid an oil shortage, continues to blatantly publish reports that sound like propaganda pieces.

“We will be fine,” it says.

All you have to do is compare its forward oil deficit projections today with what it published in June. Another quarter went by; it revised the deficits higher, changed the Q4 2026 surplus into a deficit, and then continued to forecast a 2027 surplus.

Seriously, that’s not analysis. That’s Excel drag on steroids.

And although this kind of stuff gets on my nerves, as you can probably tell from the tone of this memo, it still gives me hope that the worst is ahead of us. It’s usually never a good thing when IEA panics, because when it does, it’s probably the time to sell everything.

It’s a bit like whack-a-mole. 

First one was crude, then it was diesel, now it’s shipping.

Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply.

Ships can’t always refuel at familiar ports if they’re forced on longer journeys around Africa and diverted to the Atlantic Basin to avoid escalating hostilities near the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. That’s turned other locations into so-called bunkering hubs and driven up fuel prices.

“No one can treat bunkering as a routine, last-minute decision anymore,” said Frederik Guttormsen, Asia Pacific president at Stolt-Nielsen Ltd., an operator of 167 tankers that transport chemicals worldwide. “We’re securing fuel earlier and tracking availability and lead times at key ports because the risk is now as much about prompt supply as about price.” https://t.co/YguYPo26lQ

#CrudeOil: Brent trades around USD 105 after falling on Wednesday as concerns over Middle East supply disruptions eased and the IEA raised its forecast for the decline in global oil demand this year to 2.6 million barrels per day, while lowering expectations for next year's rebound. Following several days of Houthi attacks, it remains unclear whether Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and supply flows have suffered any meaningful setbacks. Meanwhile, the refined product market remains tight and could tighten further after Ukraine told the FT it plans to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries. Ahead of today's delayed EIA inventory report, API data showed an 11-million-barrel draw in US crude stocks, which, if confirmed, would be the largest since June 2025.
#Gold trades around USD 4,135, having recovered most of Wednesday's sharp post-CPI losses that briefly pushed prices towards, but not below, the recent low at USD 4,066. The volatile session was driven by sharp swings in US Treasury yields, initially surging on stronger-than-expected inflation before reversing abruptly as traders covered increasingly stretched short Treasury positions amid a sell-off in technology stocks. Key resistance remains around USD 4,235, a level breached during the late-September sell-off.
#Silver, meanwhile, continues to struggle for traction, partly weighed down by broader weakness across industrial metals, with #copper heading for a third consecutive daily decline. The gold-silver ratio has broken above key resistance around 72.60, now turned support, signalling renewed relative weakness in silver and raising the risk of further underperformance against gold.

US inflation reaccelerates as underlying price pressures persist.

US September CPI rose more than expected, driven partly by higher energy prices. Headline inflation accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4%, while core inflation increased to 2.6% from 2.4%. Prices also rose across several categories, including recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airfares, medical care and apparel. While some of these increases may reflect tariff-related pressures and higher energy costs, the broader rise also points to stubbornly sticky underlying inflation.

The bond market reacted sharply, with the US 10-year Treasury yield rising 9 basis points on the day, having been down 3 basis points ahead of the release. Meanwhile, futures markets are now pricing in a roughly 50% probability of a Fed rate hike as early as this month with a 25 basis point fully priced in before yearend.

Temporarily waiving sanctions on the Dark Fleet will barely move the needle if the Iranians still continue to attack tankers.

This won’t work for many reasons. First of all, it would put money directly into the hands of folks associated with the IRGC. Secondly, most of these >20yo rust buckets are too old to be allowed into ports and would not pass a safety inspection. Thirdly, if the oil isn’t loaded directly at a port, an STS transfer involving a legitimate tanker would only put that tanker on the tracking systems’ naughty lists.

And then there’s the matter of tankers being blacklisted by multiple sanctioning authorities, such as the EU, UK, Switzerland, Ukraine, etc. Those countries could still take their own actions, as we saw France do a couple of days ago. The Dark Fleet vessels themselves are not the solution, but their crews would be, given their insights into and experience with moving oil on behalf of the IRGC. They are the best asset squeeze out of the Dark Fleet, especially as tankers are being hit continuously in the SoH.
